title: What hasn't happened yet
title_target: Vad ska du göra i sommar?
goal: Talk about the future in three subtly different ways — and know when Swedish uses no future marker at all.
bekal: *ska*, *kommer att* and the present tense for the future
vocabulary for Swedish holidays and celebrations

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Planer för sommaren
dialogs.intro: Early May. Exams are only two weeks away, and the whole corridor has started talking about the same thing: summer.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Vad ska du göra i sommar?
lines.id: What are you doing this summer?
lines.literal: what shall you do in summer?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag ska jobba i juni, sedan åker jag hem till Indonesien.
lines.id: I'm working in June, then I'm going home to Indonesia.
lines.literal: I shall work in June, then go I home to Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Vad roligt! Hur länge blir du borta?
lines.id: How fun! How long will you be away?
lines.literal: what fun! how long become you away?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Sex veckor. Jag kommer tillbaka i mitten av augusti.
lines.id: Six weeks. I'm coming back in mid-August.
lines.literal: six weeks. I come back in middle-the of August.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Då missar du midsommar. Det kommer att bli tråkigt utan dig.
lines.id: Then you'll miss Midsummer. It's going to be boring without you.
lines.literal: then miss you midsummer. it comes to become boring without you.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej då, midsommar är i juni! Jag är kvar då.
lines.id: Oh no, Midsummer is in June! I'll still be here then.
lines.literal: no then, midsummer is in June! I am remaining then.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Perfekt! Då firar vi hos min faster på landet.
lines.id: Perfect! Then we'll celebrate at my aunt's in the countryside.
lines.literal: perfect! then celebrate we at my aunt on country-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Vad gör man på midsommar egentligen?
lines.id: So what do people actually do at Midsummer?
lines.literal: what does one on midsummer actually?

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Vi dansar runt en stång, äter sill och potatis, och det regnar alltid.
lines.id: We dance around a pole, eat herring and potatoes, and it always rains.
lines.literal: we dance around a pole, eat herring and potato, and it rains always.

lines.speaker: Oskar:
lines.text: Alltid. Det kommer att regna i år också. Ta med regnjacka.
lines.id: Always. It's going to rain this year too. Bring a rain jacket.
lines.literal: always. it comes to rain in year also. take with rain-jacket.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Då tar jag med paraply. Det ska bli kul!
lines.id: Then I'll bring an umbrella. It's going to be fun!
lines.literal: then take I with umbrella. it shall become fun!

notes: **Ska vs kommer att.** *Ska* is for something someone **intends or has planned**: *jag ska jobba i juni*. *Kommer att* is for something that **will happen regardless of anyone's will** — predictions, consequences, circumstances: *det kommer att regna*. The distinction is real and people notice it, even if native speakers sometimes mix them up. English draws a similar line between "I'm going to" (my plan) and "it will" (it just will).

**Sedan åker jag hem** — notice the form is **present**, not *ska åka*. When the time is already mentioned, or the plan is fixed and close, Swedish is happy with the plain present. English does exactly the same with timetables and fixed arrangements: "I fly home on Friday", "the train leaves at six".

**Det kommer att bli tråkigt** — the verb *bli* (to become) turns up constantly in future sentences, because it expresses a change of state. *Det ska bli kul* (it's going to be fun), *det blir kallt* (it'll get cold), *vi blir sena* (we'll be late).

**Midsommar** is celebrated on the Friday between 19 and 25 June, and it is Sweden's most important holiday after Christmas — for many people, more important. The whole country stops: shops close, cities empty, and everyone heads to the countryside.

**Sill** is pickled herring in all kinds of sweet-and-sour marinades, the compulsory Midsummer dish together with new potatoes, sour cream and chives. It has nothing to do with the *surströmming* from the last unit — *sill* is delicious and doesn't smell.
**Ta med** means "bring (along)", literally "take with". The particle *med* is required: *ta med paraply*, *ta med en kompis*. Without *med*, *ta* just means "take".

grammars.title: Three ways to talk about the future

head: Form
Used for
Example
Meaning
rows: fixed plans with the time stated
I'm thinking of applying for jobs.

after: The easiest way to choose: ask **who decides**. If a person decides (you, she, we), use *ska*. If nobody does — the weather, time, an unavoidable consequence — use *kommer att*.

The third row is the one used most in everyday conversation, and the one learners forget most often. If your sentence already contains *imorgon*, *på fredag* or *i sommar*, you **don't need** a future marker at all.

The past form of *ska* is **skulle**, meaning "was going to" or "would": *Jag skulle åka, men jag blev sjuk* (I was going to leave, but I got sick). It is also the polite request you already know: *skulle du kunna…?* — just like English "could you…?" sounds softer than "can you…?".

grammars.title: Making arrangements

head: Svenska
English
rows: I can't make it that day.
**Kan vi ta det på lördag istället?**

after: **Ska vi…?** is the standard way to suggest doing something in Swedish — just like English "Shall we…?" — not *vill du…?*, which sounds like an offer rather than a suggestion. *Ska vi fika?*, *Ska vi gå på bio?*, *Ska vi äta lunch?*
Swedes make plans **well in advance** and keep them. Suggesting you meet "sometime" without a date comes across as not really meaning it; proposing a date two weeks away is perfectly normal.

blocks.text: That last row is no joke: in July, most of Sweden genuinely stops working. Offices are empty, projects stall, and trying to get anything official done that month is a lost cause. Four consecutive weeks of vacation are a legal right, and almost everyone takes them at the same time.

sections.title: The weather, and why it's always the topic

blocks.text: Notice that every weather sentence uses **det** as an empty subject — exactly like *it* in English ("it's raining"). Swedish **must** have something in first position, so *det* fills it. And notice the translations: *det regnar* is both "it rains" and "it's raining" — Swedish has no separate -ing form, so the plain present covers both.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 15
items: Give the past form of ten strong verbs without looking: vara, ha, gå, komma, göra, få, se, ta, äta, dricka.
Then make three sentences with the same verb: one past, one present, one future. *Jag åt · Jag äter · Jag ska äta.*
Finally, describe your summer plans in five sentences using *ska*, *kommer att* and the present tense.
